title: Knowledge Check 3: Lessons 17-24
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 17-24 of the salesforce-architect series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: A query filters on a field that has a custom index, yet the optimizer still scans the whole table. What best explains this?
options: The index was built on a different field than the query filters on
Custom indexes only help queries that also sort on the same field
Indexes are ignored whenever the table still contains any soft-deleted rows
The filter is not selective, so an index lookup would cost more than a scan
questions.explanation: The optimizer uses an index only when the filter narrows the result set below a threshold; a broad filter makes a scan the cheaper path.

questions.question: A batch job writing archive records to a big object stops partway, with some records stored and others not. Following the recommended approach, what should the job do?
options: Commit only the rows that were written and then resume at the next row
Switch from asynchronous execution to a single synchronous transaction
Roll back the whole store and rebuild the entire archive from the start
Retry the entire batch instead of identifying which rows succeeded
questions.explanation: Because the big object store is non-transactional, a batch can partially fail, so the safe pattern is to retry the whole batch until it succeeds.

questions.question: Before moving a large set of old records out of active storage, what should the architect establish?
options: A deletion schedule so the moved records are eventually purged
A reliable retrieval path so the moved records stay findable
A custom index on the timestamp field that is being archived
A trigger that blocks future edits to the archived records
questions.explanation: Archiving is a win only if the records remain discoverable, so the query path and access pattern are designed before any data moves.

questions.question: A single transaction calls update once on a list of 12,000 records. Why does it fail?
options: The 150-statement DML limit is exceeded by the bulk call
The 10,000-row DML limit is exceeded even though one statement was issued
The 50,000-row SOQL retrieval limit is exceeded by the query
The cumulative callout timeout is exceeded by the callouts that were made
questions.explanation: Statement count and row count are separate governors: one update call is a single statement but processes 12,000 rows, past the 10,000-row ceiling.

questions.question: An org's daily API allocation is best understood as which combination?
options: A flat amount that is determined only by the org's edition
A per-user count that ignores platform license types
A fixed cap that cannot be raised by buying any more capacity
A base amount plus a per-license amount plus any add-ons
questions.explanation: The daily request budget is a base figure, plus an amount contributed by the licenses held, plus any add-ons purchased, which is why license mix drives capacity.

questions.question: Why does moving a large volume into Batch Apex succeed where one synchronous transaction failed?
options: Batch Apex raises the per-transaction DML row ceiling
Batch Apex compresses the records so that fewer rows are processed
Batch Apex disables governor limits for asynchronous code
Each chunk runs as its own transaction with a fresh set of limits
questions.explanation: The constraint was the shape of the work, not the total volume: splitting it into chunks gives each chunk its own transaction and its own fresh limits.

questions.question: Which characteristic makes a Full sandbox unsuitable as a day-to-day development environment?
options: It copies metadata only and carries no sample records
It is capped at 200 MB of data and file storage space
It cannot run the performance and load testing a release needs
It refreshes only every 29 days, so it trails the team's work
questions.explanation: A Full sandbox mirrors production but refreshes on a long cycle, so day-to-day work outpaces the copy and the environment drifts.

questions.question: A change set can move metadata between which orgs?
options: Any two orgs that share a namespace prefix
Org pairs affiliated with the same production org
Any two orgs connected by a deployment user
Orgs in different companies running the same edition
questions.explanation: A change set travels only between related orgs, meaning orgs sharing a production org, and it carries metadata rather than data records.

questions.question: Once a change set has been uploaded, what recovery does it give you if the deployment breaks production?
options: A one-click rollback to the previous deployed version
An automatic snapshot of the whole target org taken at deploy time
None built in; the prior state must be reconstructed by hand
A reverse package that the platform generates automatically
questions.explanation: Change sets keep no pre-deployment snapshot and offer no undo, so reversing a bad deployment depends on records kept outside the tool.

questions.question: Why is a machine learning release harder to manage than a plain software release?
options: Code, data, and model all ship together, and any can change
It always needs far more compute than an ordinary software build
Its outputs can never be stored in version control at all
It never needs any validation before it reaches production
questions.explanation: The artifact is a bundle rather than a single deployable, so the pipeline must handle three kinds of change plus silent model degradation on live data.

questions.question: At the most automated maturity level for machine learning operations, what does the pipeline do?
options: It retrains automatically but still deploys the trained model by hand
It builds, tests, and deploys data, model, and pipeline automatically
It deploys models but skips data and pipeline validation entirely
It runs every step of the workflow manually inside shared notebooks
questions.explanation: The fully automated level extends continuous integration and delivery to cover data and pipeline components, not just the model.

questions.question: Why does an agentic AI system call for an evaluation suite rather than exact-match tests?
options: Its outputs never vary, so each response can be checked with an exact match
It cannot be deployed to a staging environment before production
It has no training data available to validate behavior against
Its outputs are nondeterministic, so behavior is scored across many cases
questions.explanation: Because a single run never repeats, behavior is judged by scoring across a versioned set of cases instead of asserting one fixed output.

questions.question: A requirement states that the solution shall use a new custom object. How should an architect treat that clause?
options: As the underlying business why that drives every later decision
As a measurable non-functional requirement with a stated target
As a how dressed as a what, leaving the storage choice to you
As a fixed constraint that cannot be revisited
questions.explanation: The requirement only needs to state the data and its relationships; whether it lives on a custom object, a standard object, or files is the architect's call.

questions.question: What turns a non-functional requirement from a vague wish into a testable target?
options: A statement that the system should be fast and reliable
A measurable value paired with a condition, such as a time bound
A list of the technologies the delivery team prefers
A reference to the vendor framework that names the quality attribute
questions.explanation: A quality requirement is a target you can test, so it pairs a number with a condition rather than a general aspiration.

questions.question: When a stakeholder pushes for a custom path over a standard one, what does good practice require?
options: Refuse the custom path and quietly build the standard one
Accept it without comment to keep the project moving
Escalate the disagreement without recording any decision
Document the tradeoffs, the decision, and its rationale
questions.explanation: The custom path is allowed, but the architect must make the tradeoffs explicit and record the decision and its reasoning so the team can build without re-arguing it.

questions.question: Why does reviewing every change the same way undermine a design review process?
options: Teams route around it and hide the changes that matter
It slows the platform but still catches every change that ships
It removes any need to keep a written decision record
It pushes reviewers to own the delivery work themselves
questions.explanation: A review proportioned to impact works; turning it into an approval bottleneck makes teams bypass it, so real drift escapes the process.

questions.question: Which set of sections belongs in an architecture decision record?
options: Budget, schedule, staffing, and known project risks
Requirements, the full test plan, code, and deploy steps
Owner, due date, priority, and current status
Context, considered options, decision, and consequences
questions.explanation: A decision record captures the problem, the alternatives weighed, the choice, and what it makes easier or harder, so the rationale survives.

questions.question: A recorded decision has changed. What does good practice say to do?
options: Edit the original accepted record to reflect the new decision
Delete the old record so the log always stays current
Keep both records with no indication of which one is still active
Write a new record that supersedes the old one and links the two
questions.explanation: An accepted record is never edited; a superseding record preserves the history of the thinking and shows when and why the direction shifted.

questions.question: Heavy logging on a frequently accessed Apex class can cause which problem in production?
options: It permanently deletes older captured logs
It disables the org's daily API allocation
The logging itself can make the requests fail
It prevents new trace flags from being created
questions.explanation: A trace flag on a hot class or busy user adds overhead, so production debugging is done surgically with a short-lived flag on the specific path.

questions.question: Which question does Event Monitoring answer that a single debug log cannot?
options: Why one specific callout failed inside a single failing transaction
Whether a validation rule rejected a particular record
Which line of Apex threw an exception during a request
Who accessed what data, when, and from where across the org
questions.explanation: A debug log explains one transaction, while Event Monitoring provides organization-wide performance, security, and usage data to attribute activity.

questions.question: An org's API calls are rejected with a limit-exceeded error even though the daily limit is described as soft. What explains this?
options: Pushing past the soft limit trips a protection block until usage falls back
The soft limit was removed in a recent platform release
Only Bulk API calls actually count against the daily limit
The org's license tier blocks all API calls after the daily reset at midnight
questions.explanation: The daily limit allows overage, but pushing far enough trips a system protection wall that returns an error until 24-hour usage drops below the limit.

questions.question: Why can a query on an indexed field still run as a full scan?
options: Indexed fields stop being used once a table grows past a million rows
The optimizer picks between an index and a scan at random
Only queries that sort on the indexed field can use that index
A negative operator or broad filter makes the query non-selective
questions.explanation: The optimizer weighs the filter's selectivity, so an indexed field filtered with a negative or broad condition is treated as non-selective and scanned.

questions.question: Before investing in a custom index, what should the architect do?
options: Index every field that the slow query happens to filter on
Move the whole query into a scheduled batch job
Measure the field's selectivity before adding an index
Add a second filter on the same field to narrow it
questions.explanation: Indexing pays off only when the filter is selective against the threshold; indexing a low-selectivity field is wasted because the optimizer ignores it.

questions.question: When is Platform Cache the right lever?
options: For large result sets that must always stay fully up to date
For small stable values read far more often than they change
For per-user values that change on every request
For values that the application code itself mutates on every transaction
questions.explanation: Caching removes the need to run the query at all, so it fits values that are stable and hot rather than large or rapidly changing ones.
